USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

Naloxone: 4

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A physically opioid-dependent patient develops vomiting, sweating, agitation and diffuse aches immediately after naloxone. Which consequence of abrupt receptor antagonism best explains this response rather than an allergic reaction to the antagonist?

  1. Delayed accumulation with a long variable half-life
  2. Precipitated opioid withdrawal
  3. Support ventilation and obtain emergency care
  4. Recurrent toxicity after antagonist effect wanes
  5. QT prolongation and torsades risk
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Precipitated opioid withdrawal

An antagonist or high-affinity partial agonist can abruptly reduce receptor stimulation in a dependent patient.

Understanding the options

Precipitated opioid withdrawal
An antagonist or high-affinity partial agonist can abruptly reduce receptor stimulation in a dependent patient.
Support ventilation and obtain emergency care
Airway and breathing support accompany overdose reversal; naloxone does not replace resuscitation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Recurrent toxicity after antagonist effect wanes
Many opioids last longer than naloxone, so repeat dosing and monitoring may be needed. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
QT prolongation and torsades risk
Methadone can prolong repolarization; interacting medicines and electrolyte abnormalities increase concern. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Delayed accumulation with a long variable half-life
Methadone exposure and respiratory effects may accumulate beyond the apparent duration of analgesia. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
